title: John: The Word Who Tabernacled Among Us
intro:
John's Gospel is the most Jewish and the most argued-over of the four Gospels. It opens with the first words of Genesis, it is built around Israel's festivals (Passover, Sukkot, Hanukkah, the Sabbath), and it presents Jesus as the place where Israel's God now dwells: the Word, the true temple, the living water, the light of the world, the good shepherd. At the same time it contains some of the New Testament's sharpest words against 'the Jews', words that were later used to harm Jewish people. A careful reading has to hold both facts together.

The book tells us its own purpose: it was written so that readers would keep trusting that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and that by trusting they would have life in his name (John 20:31). 'Life' here is not only life after death. In John it is 'the life of the age to come' already tasted now, and it is defined relationally: knowing the one true God and Jesus whom he sent (John 17:3).

This study walks through all 21 chapters. For each one it gives the story, the historical background (who wrote, where, and what conflict lay behind it), the cultural keys (feasts, weddings, wells, shepherds, burial and crucifixion), a Jewish covenant reading, what the first hearers would have felt, what it means today, Old Testament echoes, and common misreadings. It also lays out the main scholarly views on authorship and on the book's relationship to Judaism, so you can weigh them yourself.

lens.summary: Read John as a Jewish book about Israel's God keeping covenant with his people, written in a time of painful family conflict. Its first audience heard Genesis in its opening line, Moses and the tabernacle in its talk of glory, and the festivals of Jerusalem in its middle chapters. Its big claim is that the God who once spoke creation into being, led Israel through the wilderness and dwelt in the temple has now come in person, in a Jewish man, to make his people (and through them the world) his friends. 'Believing' in John means ongoing trust and loyalty, a relationship, not a single mental assent. And the book's harsh words about 'the Jews' belong to an argument inside the Jewish family, mostly aimed at Judean leaders, not to a verdict on the Jewish people.

principles.name: Genesis and the Word
principles.text: 'In the beginning' deliberately echoes Gen 1:1. God's Word (Hebrew dabar, Aramaic memra) and Wisdom were already ways Jews spoke of God acting in the world. John says that this Word is personal and has become flesh. A Jewish hearer would recognise the categories before being startled by the claim.

principles.name: Temple and tabernacle
principles.text: 'The Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us' (John 1:14) recalls the tabernacle in the wilderness and the glory cloud that filled it. Throughout John, Jesus' body is the new meeting place of God and people (John 2:21), so the loss of the Jerusalem temple in AD 70 is answered, not ignored.

principles.name: The festivals as the stage
principles.text: Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for Passover, Sukkot (Tabernacles) and Hanukkah (Dedication), and heals on the Sabbath. At each feast he takes up its central symbols (bread, water, light, the consecrated temple, rest) and says they find their meaning in him. Jesus is not opposed to Israel's calendar; he keeps it, as a faithful Jew, and fills it.

principles.name: 'I AM' and the one God of Israel
principles.text: Jesus' 'I am' sayings echo how God names himself in Exod 3:14 and especially in Isaiah (Isa 43:10, Isa 43:25), where 'I am he' is the language of Israel's one God. John is not leaving Jewish monotheism behind; he is claiming Jesus belongs inside the identity of the one God of the Shema (Deut 6:4).

principles.name: Life of the age to come, known in relationship
principles.text: Zōē aiōnios is usually translated 'eternal life', but in Jewish idiom it is 'the life of the age to come' (Dan 12:2). John's surprise is that this future life starts now, and he defines it as knowing God (John 17:3). In Hebrew thought 'knowing' is covenant intimacy, not just information.

principles.name: Believing as trusting loyalty
principles.text: John never uses the noun 'faith' (pistis); he uses the verb 'believe/trust' (pisteuō) about 98 times. It is something you keep doing. Characters move toward or away from Jesus over time (Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman, the blind man, Thomas). Trust is a journey of relationship, often shown by 'remaining' (menō) with Jesus.

principles.name: 'The Jews' as an intramural word
principles.text: Hoi Ioudaioi can mean Judeans (people of Judea, as opposed to Galileans), the Jewish people, or, very often in John, the religious authorities in Jerusalem who oppose Jesus. Jesus, his mother, all the disciples and the narrator's first community were Jews. The harsh language reflects a bitter family quarrel, not a charge against the Jewish people of any age.

principles.name: Shepherds, friends and family
principles.text: John's picture of salvation is relational: God's children born 'from above' (John 1:12-13), sheep who know the shepherd's voice (John 10:14), servants made friends (John 15:15), and a new family formed at the cross (John 19:26-27). This is covenant language from Ezekiel 34 and Jeremiah 31 made personal.

audienceMap.group: Jewish followers of Jesus, some pushed out of synagogue life
audienceMap.concerns: Grief and anger at losing their place among family and neighbours; wondering whether following Jesus meant losing the festivals, Torah and temple; needing assurance that Jesus is truly Israel's Messiah (John 9:22, John 16:2).

audienceMap.group: Gentile believers in a city such as Ephesus
audienceMap.concerns: Learning the Jewish story they had joined; hearing that they are the 'other sheep' brought into one flock (John 10:16); needing explanations of Hebrew terms, which John supplies (John 1:38, John 1:41).

audienceMap.group: Secret sympathisers still in the synagogue
audienceMap.concerns: Like Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea, people who believed but feared open loyalty (John 12:42); the Gospel invites them to step into the light (John 19:38-39).
The Gospel repeatedly says the Baptist was not the light but a witness to it (John 1:8, John 3:30); some scholars think Baptist loyalists were part of the audience (compare Acts 19:1-7 at Ephesus).

audienceMap.group: Believers drawn to a 'spiritual' Christ without real flesh
audienceMap.concerns: Early docetic ideas (that Jesus only seemed to be human) may lie behind the stress on flesh, blood, water, tears and touchable wounds (John 1:14, John 19:34, John 20:27); 1 John 4:2 confronts this directly.

argument.label: The Word becomes flesh
argument.text: The prologue retells Genesis 1: the Word who was with God and was God has come into the world, pitched his tent among Israel and shown the Father's glory, full of covenant love and faithfulness (John 1:14, compare Exod 34:6).

argument.label: Witnesses and first disciples
argument.text: John the Baptist points to the Lamb of God; disciples follow and receive Jewish titles for Jesus: Rabbi, Messiah, the one Moses wrote about, King of Israel, Son of Man.

argument.label: Book of Signs: seven signs
argument.text: Seven signs reveal who Jesus is: water to wine (2), the official's son (4), the paralysed man (5), feeding the 5,000 (6), walking on water (6), the man born blind (9), the raising of Lazarus (11). Each provokes faith in some and resistance in others.

argument.label: New temple, new birth, true worship
argument.text: Jesus clears the temple and speaks of his body as the temple; he tells Nicodemus of birth from above and the Samaritan woman of worship in Spirit and truth. Old institutions are not mocked but fulfilled.

argument.label: Jesus at Israel's feasts
argument.text: Sabbath (5), Passover (6), Sukkot (7-9) and Hanukkah (10): at each festival Jesus claims its symbols — Sabbath work, manna, water, light, the consecrated one — and controversy with the Jerusalem authorities grows.

argument.label: Lazarus and the decision to kill
argument.text: The greatest sign, Lazarus raised, triggers the council's decision that one man should die for the nation. Jesus is anointed for burial, enters Jerusalem as king, and the hour arrives. The Book of Signs closes with Isaiah's words about unbelief.

argument.label: Book of Glory begins
argument.text: On the eve of Passover Jesus washes his disciples' feet, gives the new commandment of love, and predicts betrayal and denial. Glory in John is shown by humble self-giving.

argument.label: Farewell discourse and prayer
argument.text: Like Jacob or Moses before death, Jesus gives a farewell speech: the Father's house, the Paraclete (Spirit), the vine and branches, coming persecution, and his prayer that the disciples be one and share God's love.

argument.label: Arrest, trial and the lifted-up king
argument.text: Jesus goes to death in control: 'I am' in the garden, a king before Pilate, crucified as the Passover lambs are slaughtered, saying 'It is finished', buried as a king with lavish spices.

argument.label: Risen Lord, sending Spirit
argument.text: Mary Magdalene meets the risen Jesus in a garden; he breathes the Spirit on the disciples as God breathed into Adam; Thomas confesses 'My Lord and my God'.

argument.label: Purpose: believe and have life
argument.text: John 20:30-31 states the aim: these signs are written so that you may keep trusting that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and have life in his name.

argument.label: Epilogue: Peter restored, witness sealed
argument.text: By the Sea of Galilee Jesus feeds the disciples, restores Peter with three questions of love and commissions him to shepherd; the Beloved Disciple's testimony is affirmed as true.

chapters.title: The Word, the Lamb and the first disciples
chapters.summary: John opens 'in the beginning' with the Word who was with God and was God, through whom everything was made. The Word is life and light; the world did not recognise him and his own people largely did not receive him, but those who did became God's children. The Word became flesh and 'tabernacled' among us, full of grace and truth. Then the story begins: John the Baptist denies being the Messiah, Elijah or the Prophet, and points to Jesus as 'the Lamb of God'. Andrew, Peter, Philip and Nathanael follow, giving Jesus a cascade of titles: Rabbi, Messiah, the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, Son of God, King of Israel. Jesus promises they will see angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man.
chapters.background:
Who wrote this? The book itself only says its witness is 'the disciple whom Jesus loved' (John 21:20-24). Irenaeus, around AD 180, said this was John son of Zebedee, who published the Gospel at Ephesus in old age. Many modern scholars think the Gospel took shape in stages within a community gathered around this disciple, finished around AD 90. Richard Bauckham argues the Beloved Disciple was a Jerusalem disciple called John the Elder, whom the early writer Papias mentions alongside the apostles.

Ephesus was a large Greek city in Asia Minor (modern Turkey) with a substantial Jewish community, and Acts records that disciples of John the Baptist were there (Acts 19:1-7). That may explain why chapter 1 is so careful to say the Baptist was a witness, not the light (John 1:8). The Jerusalem temple had been destroyed by Rome in AD 70, so a Gospel that calls Jesus God's 'tabernacle' would speak to a grieving people.
chapters.culture:
'Word' (logos) worked in two worlds at once. For Greek listeners, Stoic philosophers spoke of the Logos as the reason ordering the universe. For Jewish listeners, God created by speaking (Gen 1:3), his word 'ran swiftly' (Ps 147:15), Wisdom was beside him at creation (Prov 8:30), and the Aramaic Targums (synagogue paraphrases of scripture) often spoke of God's Memra (Word) acting in creation and history. The Jewish philosopher Philo of Alexandria, a contemporary of Jesus, called the Logos God's 'firstborn' and even a 'second God'.

The Baptist's questioners are priests and Levites sent from Jerusalem (John 1:19) — the temple establishment checking a rival movement. 'Lamb of God' would evoke the Passover lamb, the daily temple lambs and the servant led like a lamb to slaughter (Isa 53:7). 'Come and see' and 'where are you staying?' reflect how disciples attached themselves to a rabbi: by living with him.
chapters.jewishLens:
The prologue is best heard as a Jewish meditation on Genesis 1 and on the Exodus. Light shines in darkness as at creation; the Word 'tabernacles' as God's glory filled the tent in the wilderness (Exod 40:34-35); 'grace and truth' echoes God's self-description to Moses as 'abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness' (Exod 34:6). Moses could not see God's face (Exod 33:20), but the only Son 'who is at the Father's side' has made him known (John 1:18).

Daniel Boyarin, a Jewish scholar of the Talmud, argues that the idea of a divine Word alongside God was not foreign to first-century Jews; what made John distinctive was saying this Word became a particular human being. 'His own' who did not receive him (John 1:11) are first of all Israel, yet the receivers are also Israelites — Andrew, Peter, Nathanael, 'an Israelite in whom there is no deceit'. Jacob's ladder (Gen 28:12) is applied to Jesus: he is the new Bethel, the 'house of God', where heaven and earth meet.
chapters.audience: Jewish believers who had lost the temple and, perhaps, their synagogue would hear: God's presence has not left you; it has been among you in a person. Gentile hearers would hear that the reason behind the universe has a name and a face. Followers of the Baptist would hear their teacher himself saying 'he must increase'. And everyone would hear an invitation to the same simple step the first disciples took: 'come and see'.
chapters.today: The prologue resists both a merely human Jesus and a ghostly, unreal one. God is known not first through ideas but through a life lived in flesh. And discipleship begins as it did for Andrew: by spending time with Jesus and then bringing a brother.

echoes.note: 'In the beginning', light and darkness, creation by speech.
Glory filling the tent: the Word 'tabernacled' among us.
'Steadfast love and faithfulness' behind 'grace and truth'.
The voice in the wilderness preparing the Lord's way.
Jacob's ladder: angels ascending and descending, now on the Son of Man.

misread.popular: John's Logos is a borrowing from Greek philosophy, so the prologue is a 'Greek' introduction to an un-Jewish Gospel.
misread.better: The prologue is rooted in Genesis, Wisdom and Exodus; Greek hearers would catch resonance, but its world is Jewish (Brown, Keener, Boyarin).

chapters.title: Wine at Cana, fire in the temple
chapters.summary: At a wedding in Cana of Galilee the wine runs out. Jesus' mother tells him; he says his hour has not yet come, but she tells the servants to do whatever he says. Jesus has six stone water jars, used for Jewish purification, filled to the brim — about 120 to 180 gallons — and the water becomes excellent wine. This is 'the first of his signs', revealing his glory, and his disciples trust him. Then at Passover in Jerusalem Jesus drives out the animal sellers and money changers from the temple courts. Asked for a sign, he says, 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.' John explains he meant the temple of his body, which the disciples understood only after the resurrection.
chapters.background: John places the temple action at the start of Jesus' ministry, while Matthew, Mark and Luke place it in the last week. Scholars debate whether there were two incidents or whether John moved it to the front for theological reasons, to frame the whole ministry with the replacement of the temple by Jesus' body. Writing after AD 70, John's readers knew the temple had in fact been destroyed. 'Forty-six years' to build this temple (John 2:20) fits Herod's rebuilding begun around 20/19 BC, pointing to about AD 27/28.
chapters.culture:
Jewish weddings in Galilee could last up to a week, and the groom's family hosted. Running out of wine was a serious public shame: hospitality and honour were bound up with providing for guests, and some scholars suggest gifts of wine created reciprocal obligations. Mary's 'they have no wine' is a request made on behalf of the family.

The six stone jars matter. Stone, unlike pottery, was believed not to contract ritual impurity, and stone vessels have been found widely in first-century Judea and Galilee, including near Cana. They held water for hand-washing and purification. Jesus does not pour the water out; he transforms it. In the temple, money changers exchanged coins into the Tyrian shekel required for the temple tax, and animals were sold for pilgrims who could not bring their own. The trade was legal and useful; Jesus' protest is about it filling the space of prayer and turning 'my Father's house' into a marketplace.
chapters.jewishLens:
Abundant wine was a prophetic picture of the messianic age: 'the mountains shall drip sweet wine' (Amos 9:13), and the Lord would make a feast of 'well-aged wines' for all peoples (Isa 25:6). A wedding was itself an image of God and Israel (Isa 62:4-5). So the first sign announces that the long-promised feast has begun, using Israel's own purification jars as the containers of the new.

In the temple Jesus acts like a prophet. The disciples recall 'zeal for your house will consume me' (Ps 69:9), and Zechariah had foreseen a day when there would no longer be a trader in the house of the Lord (Zech 14:21). His word about raising the temple in three days makes his body the true meeting place of God and people. This is not contempt for the temple: Jesus calls it 'my Father's house'. It is the claim that what the temple pointed to is now present in him.
chapters.audience: For Jewish readers after AD 70, the question 'where do we meet God now?' was raw. John answers: in the risen body of Jesus. The wedding scene also reassured them that following Jesus was not a sad loss of Jewish life but joy overflowing from within it — the jars of purification filled with wine.
chapters.today: Jesus' first sign is an act of kindness that spares a family shame at a party. The God of John is generous and joyful. The temple scene warns religious communities whenever worship becomes business, and points to Jesus himself as the centre of worship.

echoes.note: Mountains dripping with wine in the restored age.
God's feast of fine wines for all peoples.
'Zeal for your house will consume me.'
No more traders in the house of the Lord on that day.
'Do whatever he tells you' — Pharaoh's words about Joseph, echoed by Mary.

misread.popular: The temple cleansing shows Jesus rejecting Jewish religion and its sacrifices as dead ritual.
misread.better: Jesus defends 'my Father's house' like the prophets did; his body becomes the temple's fulfilment, not a condemnation of Israel's worship (Coloe, Keener).

chapters.title: Nicodemus: birth from above and the lifted-up Son
chapters.summary: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and member of the ruling council, comes to Jesus at night and calls him a teacher from God. Jesus tells him no one can see God's kingdom without being born anōthen — 'again' or 'from above'. Nicodemus takes it literally; Jesus speaks of being born of water and Spirit, and of the Spirit as wind blowing where it wills. Jesus says the Son of Man must be lifted up as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so that whoever trusts may have eternal life — 'for God so loved the world'. Light has come, and people reveal themselves by coming to it or avoiding it. The chapter ends with John the Baptist rejoicing as 'the friend of the bridegroom': 'He must increase, but I must decrease.'
chapters.background: Nicodemus is one of John's most carefully drawn characters. He appears three times: coming by night (John 3:2), cautiously defending Jesus in the council (John 7:50-51), and finally bringing about 75 pounds of spices for Jesus' burial (John 19:39). Many scholars think he represented a group in John's own day: synagogue members who were sympathetic to Jesus but afraid to say so openly (John 12:42). The dialogue slides from Jesus' voice into the narrator's reflection, and translations disagree where the quotation marks end (after 3:15 or 3:21).
chapters.culture: Visiting a teacher at night was not necessarily cowardly; rabbis were known to study Torah at night. But in John, night and darkness carry symbolic weight (John 13:30). 'The teacher of Israel' marks Nicodemus as a recognised scholar. The 'friend of the bridegroom' (John 3:29) was the groom's best man, who arranged the wedding and rejoiced at the groom's joy, not seeking the bride for himself.
chapters.jewishLens:
Jesus expects 'the teacher of Israel' to understand (John 3:10), which points us to Israel's scriptures. Ezekiel promised that God would sprinkle clean water on his people and put a new spirit within them (Ezek 36:25-27), and in the valley of dry bones the 'wind/breath/spirit' (ruach) would bring dead Israel to life (Ezek 37:9-14). 'Born of water and Spirit' is that promised renewal.

Then Jesus turns to Numbers 21. When the people were dying from snake bites, God told Moses to set a bronze serpent on a pole; whoever looked at it lived. Jewish tradition (for example the Wisdom of Solomon 16:6-7 and the Mishnah, Rosh Hashanah 3:8) stressed that it was not the bronze that healed but turning the heart to God. 'Lifted up' (hypsoō) in John means both crucified and exalted (John 12:32-33). John 3:16 explains the logic: God loved the world 'in this way' — by giving his Son to be lifted up so the dying could look and live.
chapters.audience: Secret believers would recognise themselves in Nicodemus and be gently urged toward the light. All hearers would be reminded that new life is God's gift, as surprising as the wind, and that it arrives through the cross, just as healing came to Israel in the wilderness through what God provided.
chapters.today: The famous verse lives inside a story of a cautious, honest seeker who takes years to step into the open. God's love is costly and wide, embracing 'the world', and new birth is something God does, not a technique we perform.

Clean water and a new spirit for Israel.

'Your only son, whom you love' — the giving of a beloved son.

misread.popular: John 3:16 stands alone as a summary: believe and you go to heaven when you die; 'born again' means praying a decision prayer.
misread.better: 3:16 completes 3:14-15 (the lifted-up serpent); 'eternal life' is the life of the age to come, starting now; new birth 'from above' is the Spirit's renewal promised in Ezekiel (Keener, Thompson, Carson).

chapters.title: Living water at Jacob's well
chapters.summary: Travelling through Samaria, a tired Jesus sits by Jacob's well at noon and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink — breaking norms of gender, ethnicity and purity. He offers 'living water' that becomes a spring welling up to eternal life. He shows he knows her history of five husbands, and she raises the old dispute: should God be worshipped on this mountain (Gerizim) or in Jerusalem? Jesus says salvation is from the Jews, yet the hour is coming when true worshippers will worship the Father in Spirit and truth. She says the Messiah is coming; Jesus answers, 'I am he, the one speaking to you.' She leaves her water jar and brings her town, and many Samaritans believe, calling him 'Saviour of the world'. Back in Cana, Jesus heals a royal official's son with a word: the second sign.
chapters.background: Jews and Samaritans shared descent from Israel and the five books of Moses, but had been divided for centuries. Samaritans worshipped on Mount Gerizim; the Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed their temple there in the late second century BC (Josephus places it around 128 BC; excavations suggest about 111-110 BC), and bitterness ran deep. The narrator explains 'Jews do not share things in common with Samaritans' (John 4:9), suggesting some readers needed this explained. Acts 8 shows Samaritans responding to the gospel early, and some scholars think Samaritan believers were part of John's community.
chapters.culture:
Wells were meeting places, and in Israel's stories they are where future marriages begin: Abraham's servant meets Rebekah (Gen 24), Jacob meets Rachel (Gen 29), Moses meets Zipporah (Exod 2:15-21). A first audience would sense a 'betrothal scene' — but here it becomes a bond between Jesus and a whole people. 'Living water' meant running water from a spring, as opposed to still cistern water; it was the purest kind for purification.

Why noon? Some say she was avoiding other women out of shame; others note noon is simply when a traveller would rest, and that the text never calls her immoral. Five husbands may reflect widowhood, divorce by men (women could rarely initiate divorce) or levirate marriage; the current man may be a relative supporting her. Jesus' word reveals knowledge, not condemnation, and she becomes the first evangelist to a town.
chapters.jewishLens:
Jesus speaks as a Jew — 'we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews' (John 4:22) — while opening the door to Samaritans as part of a restored Israel. The prophets hoped for the reunion of the northern tribes with Judah (Ezek 37:15-22). God himself is 'the fountain of living waters' (Jer 2:13), and the end-time temple would send out life-giving water (Ezek 47:1-12). Jesus offers that water personally.

The Samaritans expected the Taheb, a prophet like Moses (Deut 18:15-18), rather than a Davidic king. Jesus' 'I am he' (egō eimi) is the first of John's 'I am' sayings. Worship 'in Spirit and truth' does not reject place out of contempt; it means the Father seeks worshippers wherever they are, because the true temple is now Jesus himself.
chapters.audience: A mixed community of Jews, Samaritans and Gentiles in John's day would hear its own story: the enmity of centuries dissolved around one well. A royal official (probably serving Herod Antipas) trusting Jesus' word without seeing anticipates the Gentile believers 'who have not seen and yet believe' (John 20:29).
chapters.today: Jesus crosses lines of shame, gender and old religious hatred, treats a marginal woman as a theological conversation partner, and makes her a witness. True worship is not owned by any one place or group.

Jacob's land at Shechem, near Sychar.
God the fountain of living waters.

Origins of the Samaritan population and its mixed worship.

misread.popular: The Samaritan woman was a notorious sinner whose sexual immorality Jesus exposed.
misread.better: The text never calls her sinful; her marriages may reflect widowhood or divorce. She is a seeker and the first to bring a town to Jesus (Levine, Keener, Lynn Cohick).

chapters.title: Healing on the Sabbath and the Son who works like the Father
chapters.summary: At 'a feast of the Jews' Jesus visits the pool of Bethesda in Jerusalem with its five porches, where many sick people lie. He asks a man paralysed for 38 years, 'Do you want to be well?', and tells him to pick up his mat and walk. It is the Sabbath, so the authorities object to the man carrying his mat. When they learn Jesus healed him, they challenge Jesus, who answers: 'My Father is working until now, and I am working.' They seek to kill him because he calls God his own Father, 'making himself equal with God'. Jesus explains that the Son does only what he sees the Father doing, has authority to give life and to judge, and that witnesses testify for him: John the Baptist, his works, the Father, the scriptures and Moses.
chapters.background: For a long time some scholars doubted the pool of Bethesda with five porticoes existed, and treated the detail as symbolic (five books of Moses). Excavations near the Church of St Anne in Jerusalem uncovered a large double pool with a dividing wall, giving four sides plus a middle colonnade: five porches. This is often cited as evidence of the Gospel writer's accurate local knowledge, and the Copper Scroll from Qumran may mention a site called Beth Eshdatayin ('house of the twin pools'). John 5:3b-4 (an angel stirring the water) is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is usually printed in footnotes.
chapters.culture: Sabbath was Israel's weekly gift of rest and a sign of the covenant (Exod 31:13-17). Carrying loads from one domain to another was among the activities rabbis classed as work (Jer 17:21-22 already forbids carrying burdens through Jerusalem's gates on the Sabbath), so the objection was a reasonable application of Torah, not pettiness. Jewish teachers also discussed whether God himself rests on the Sabbath; since people are born and die every Sabbath, they agreed God continues to give life and to judge — the very two works Jesus claims (John 5:21-22).
chapters.jewishLens:
Jesus does not attack the Sabbath; he enters a Jewish debate about God's own Sabbath work and places himself on God's side of it. In Jewish law an agent (shaliach) acts with the authority of the one who sends him; Jesus speaks as the Son-agent who does exactly what the Father does. Yet 'honour the Son as they honour the Father' (John 5:23) goes beyond an ordinary agent. The 'Son of Man' who receives authority to judge echoes Dan 7:13-14, and the hour when the dead hear his voice echoes Dan 12:2.

The appeal to witnesses follows Deut 19:15: truth is established by two or three witnesses. Moses himself, the great intercessor, will be a witness for Jesus because 'he wrote of me' (John 5:46).
chapters.audience: A community accused of breaking with Moses would hear Jesus claim that Moses and the scriptures were on his side. They would also hear that the conflict over the Sabbath was a debate about who Jesus is, not about whether God's law is good.
chapters.today: 'Do you want to be well?' is a disarmingly personal question. Jesus' Sabbath healings show God's rest as restoration. The chapter also warns that it is possible to search the scriptures diligently yet miss the person they point to (John 5:39-40).

Not carrying burdens on the Sabbath.
The Son of Man given authority.

misread.popular: Jesus broke the Sabbath to show that God's law was legalistic and obsolete.
misread.better: Jesus engages a Jewish debate about God's life-giving work on the Sabbath and claims to share it; the issue is his identity, not the law's worth (Keener, Levine, Thompson).

chapters.title: Bread of life at Passover
chapters.summary: Near Passover, by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus feeds five thousand people with five barley loaves and two fish, and twelve baskets of leftovers are gathered. The crowd says he is 'the Prophet who is to come' and wants to make him king by force, so he withdraws. That night the disciples see him walking on the sea; he says 'I am; do not be afraid.' In the synagogue at Capernaum Jesus says he is the bread of life, the true bread from heaven, greater than the manna; whoever eats his flesh and drinks his blood has eternal life. Many disciples find this 'a hard saying' and leave. Jesus asks the Twelve if they will go too; Peter answers, 'Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.'
chapters.background: This is the second Passover in John (John 2:13, John 6:4, John 11:55), which is why many say Jesus' ministry lasted about three years. The feeding is the only miracle besides the resurrection found in all four Gospels. The language of eating flesh and drinking blood is widely seen as connected to the Lord's Supper, which John does not narrate at the Last Supper; how directly John means the Eucharist is debated (Catholic and Orthodox readers see a clear reference; many Protestants read it as a vivid image for trusting Jesus' death, see John 6:35 and John 6:47).
chapters.culture: Barley loaves were the bread of the poor. The crowd's response follows Passover logic: Passover remembered the exodus, and many Jews hoped the Messiah would come at Passover and that the manna would fall again in the messianic age (2 Baruch 29:8 speaks of manna descending again). A 'prophet like Moses' who fed people in the wilderness was exactly what such hopes looked for. Eating someone's 'flesh' and drinking 'blood' would shock: Torah forbade consuming blood (Lev 17:10-14). Jesus' language is deliberately jarring.
chapters.jewishLens:
The chapter is a Passover midrash. The crowd quotes 'He gave them bread from heaven to eat' (Ps 78:24, compare Exod 16:4), and Jesus interprets it like a synagogue teacher: it was not Moses but my Father who gives the true bread from heaven. In Jewish tradition Torah and Wisdom were spoken of as bread: Wisdom invites, 'Come, eat of my bread' (Prov 9:5), and Isaiah calls the thirsty and hungry to come and eat without cost (Isa 55:1-3). Jesus presents himself as God's living Torah-Wisdom-bread.

Walking on the sea with 'I am; do not be afraid' echoes God who 'trampled the waves of the sea' (Job 9:8) and led Israel through the sea at the exodus (Ps 77:19). The grumbling (gongyzō) of the crowd (John 6:41) echoes Israel's murmuring in the wilderness (Exod 16:2). Peter's confession, 'the Holy One of God', is a Jewish title for one set apart by God.
chapters.audience: The scene of disciples leaving would resonate with a community that had seen others turn back. Peter's 'to whom shall we go?' spoke for those who stayed despite the cost. Readers who celebrated the Lord's Supper would hear their meal echoed.
chapters.today: Jesus offers himself, not just his gifts. Some follow for loaves; real discipleship is staying when the teaching is hard, because there is nowhere else to find life.

misread.popular: Readers either flatten John 6 into a doctrine of the Mass, or dismiss any sacramental meaning as pure metaphor.
misread.better: The chapter is first a Passover-manna midrash about trusting Jesus as God's bread; whether and how it points to the Eucharist is a genuine debate between traditions (Brown, Carson, Keener).

chapters.title: Sukkot: rivers of living water
chapters.summary: At the feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot) Jesus' brothers, who do not believe in him, urge him to show himself in Judea. He goes up quietly, then teaches openly in the temple halfway through the feast. People argue: is he a good man or a deceiver? Has he studied? Is he the Messiah? Can the Messiah come from Galilee? On the last great day of the feast Jesus stands and cries out, 'If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the scripture said, out of his heart will flow rivers of living water' — which John explains as the Spirit. The temple guards fail to arrest him ('No one ever spoke like this man'), and Nicodemus urges a fair hearing.
chapters.background: Chapters 7 to 10:21 are set at Sukkot, the autumn feast. The debate over Jesus' origin (Galilee, Bethlehem, unknown) reflects real Jewish discussions about how the Messiah would appear (John 7:27, John 7:42). Fear 'of the Jews' among people who are themselves Jews (John 7:13) shows that 'the Jews' here means the Jerusalem authorities. The fact that even Jesus' brothers did not believe (John 7:5) is a striking admission that early Christians would hardly invent; James later became a leader in Jerusalem (Gal 1:19).
chapters.culture: Sukkot was the most joyful pilgrimage feast. Families lived in booths for seven days, remembering the wilderness (Lev 23:42-43), and gave thanks for the harvest. According to the Mishnah (Sukkah 4-5), each morning a priest drew water from the pool of Siloam in a golden pitcher and processed to the temple, where it was poured on the altar with wine while the Hallel Psalms (Ps 113-118) were sung. It was also a prayer for the coming winter rains. The rabbis said whoever had not seen the rejoicing of the water-drawing had never seen joy. On the seventh day, the priests circled the altar seven times. Into that scene Jesus cries, 'Come to me and drink.'
chapters.jewishLens:
The water ritual looked back to water from the rock in the wilderness (Exod 17:6, Ps 78:15-16) and forward to the end-time river flowing from the temple (Ezek 47:1-12) and the living waters going out from Jerusalem on the day when all nations would keep Sukkot (Zech 14:8, Zech 14:16). Isaiah tied it together: 'With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation' (Isa 12:3), and God promised to pour water on the thirsty and his Spirit on Israel's offspring (Isa 44:3).

Jesus claims that the hope of the feast is fulfilled in him: from him (or from the believer, the Greek can be read either way) flow rivers of the Spirit. He is standing at the heart of Israel's worship, using its own words, at its own feast. The debate about him is a Jewish debate among Jews about the Messiah.
chapters.audience: Readers far from Jerusalem, possibly cut off from festival life, would hear that the joy and the Spirit promised at Sukkot had not been taken from them: they flowed from Jesus. The divided crowd also mirrored their own experience of families split over Jesus.
chapters.today: The Spirit is not an abstract doctrine but the satisfaction of a deep thirst. The chapter also shows honest uncertainty about Jesus, and Nicodemus models a quiet courage: insisting on fairness when a group rushes to judgement.

chapters.title: The light of the world and 'before Abraham was, I am'
chapters.summary: Most modern Bibles first print the story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53-8:11) in brackets: Jesus writes on the ground, says 'Let the one without sin cast the first stone', and sends her away uncondemned, 'go and sin no more'. Then, still at Sukkot, Jesus says, 'I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness.' A long, increasingly heated debate follows about his testimony, his Father and his origin. To Jews who had believed in him, he says the truth will set them free; they protest that as Abraham's children they have never been slaves. The argument escalates to Jesus' charge that their desire to kill him shows the devil's parentage, not Abraham's. It climaxes in 'Before Abraham was, I am', and they pick up stones.
chapters.background: The adultery story is missing from the earliest Greek manuscripts (such as P66, P75, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus), and in some later manuscripts it appears in other places, even in Luke. Most scholars, conservative and critical, think it was not part of John's original text, though many believe it preserves a genuine early tradition about Jesus. The rest of the chapter is the sharpest conflict in the Gospel, and its polemic has been abused more than almost any other text. Scholars widely believe its harshness reflects the bitter later conflict between John's community and synagogue leaders as well as the original setting.
chapters.culture:
During Sukkot, according to the Mishnah (Sukkah 5:2-4), four huge golden lamp-stands were lit in the Court of the Women in the temple. It was said that no courtyard in Jerusalem was not lit by their light, and devout men danced with torches through the night while Levites played music on the fifteen steps. Jesus speaks 'in the treasury' (John 8:20), which was in that same court. To say 'I am the light of the world' there was like pointing to the blazing lamps and saying, 'This is about me.'

Arguments about descent ('we are Abraham's children') were arguments about honour and identity. In ancient thought you resembled your father: actions revealed parentage.
chapters.jewishLens:
The light recalls the pillar of fire that guided Israel in the wilderness (Exod 13:21), the very event Sukkot remembers, and Isaiah's servant as 'a light to the nations' (Isa 49:6). 'Before Abraham was, I am' echoes God's own name (Exod 3:14) and especially the 'I am he' of Isaiah (Isa 43:10-13), spoken by the one God who existed before all. The hearers understand it as a claim to divine identity, which is why they reach for stones as for blasphemy (Lev 24:16).

The 'children of the devil' language is family polemic. The Dead Sea Scrolls divide even Israel into 'sons of light' and 'sons of darkness'; the prophets called Israel's leaders 'rulers of Sodom' (Isa 1:10). Jesus is speaking to particular people seeking his death (John 8:40), using the logic that you show your father by your deeds, the same test 1 John 3:8-10 applies to Christians. It is not a statement about the Jewish people.
chapters.audience: John's community, in conflict with synagogue leaders, would hear their own arguments about Abraham, Moses and freedom. They would hear that Jesus is the light the Sukkot lamps celebrated. Later readers who were no longer a vulnerable minority would misuse the same words with terrible results.
chapters.today: This chapter must be read with great care. It is a picture of Jesus revealing God's light and of truth that frees people from the slavery of sin, not a licence for contempt. The adultery story, whatever its textual history, shows Jesus protecting a vulnerable woman from a crowd and still calling her to a new life.

misread.popular: John 8:44 shows that Jews are children of the devil — a reading used in medieval and modern antisemitism.
misread.better: Jesus addresses particular opponents seeking to kill him, using Jewish family polemic; the same test applies to anyone (1 John 3:8-10). It cannot rightly be applied to the Jewish people (Brown, Keener, Levine; Reinhartz warns of its real anti-Jewish effect).

chapters.title: The man born blind and the fear of being put out
chapters.summary: Jesus' disciples ask whether a man born blind was punished for his own sin or his parents'. Jesus says neither: it is so God's works may be revealed. He spits on the ground, makes mud, anoints the man's eyes and sends him to wash in the pool of Siloam ('Sent'). He comes back seeing. It is the Sabbath. The neighbours, the Pharisees and the man's parents are questioned; the parents answer cautiously because 'the Jews had already agreed that anyone who confessed Jesus to be Messiah would be put out of the synagogue' (John 9:22). The man grows bolder in each interview, from 'the man called Jesus' to 'a prophet' to worshipping Jesus as the Son of Man. He is thrown out. Jesus finds him and says he came so the blind might see and those who claim to see become blind.
chapters.background:
John 9:22 is the first of three aposynagōgos ('put out of the synagogue') passages (also John 12:42 and John 16:2). In 1968 J. Louis Martyn proposed that John 9 should be read on two levels: the story of Jesus and the experience of John's community decades later, expelled from the synagogue. Martyn linked this to the Birkat ha-Minim, the 'blessing' (in fact a curse) against heretics in the Jewish daily prayer, said to have been revised at Yavneh around AD 85.

This theory has been widely debated. Reuven Kimelman (1981) and others showed there is no clear evidence that the first-century form targeted Christians, or that it was used empire-wide to expel them; the text mentioning Nazarenes (notzrim) comes from later manuscripts. Joel Marcus (2009) defends a modified version. Adele Reinhartz questions the expulsion theory itself. Most scholars today accept that some Jesus-followers experienced exclusion from local synagogues, but not a single, official decree.

The pool of Siloam from the Second Temple period was rediscovered in Jerusalem in 2004, a large stepped pool consistent with ritual washing.
chapters.culture: Many people assumed disability was punishment for sin, a view the book of Job had already challenged. Spittle was regarded in the ancient world as having healing power, and making mud could count as kneading, one of the activities forbidden on the Sabbath in later rabbinic lists. Synagogue membership meant much more than a weekly service: it was family, community, trade, burial and social belonging. Being 'put out' meant social death. The parents' fear is entirely understandable.
chapters.jewishLens:
Opening the eyes of the blind was a sign of God's new age (Isa 35:5, Isa 42:7). Jesus as 'the light of the world' (John 9:5) continues the Sukkot theme, and Siloam was the pool from which the Sukkot water was drawn. Making clay and anointing may echo God forming Adam from the ground (Gen 2:7): a new creation for a man born blind.

The debate among the Pharisees is a genuine Jewish argument: some say 'This man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath', but others ask, 'How can a sinner do such signs?' (John 9:16). The man reasons like a Torah student: 'God does not listen to sinners... if this man were not from God, he could do nothing' (John 9:31-33). The issue is the true reading of Moses.
chapters.audience: For a community that had paid the price of exclusion, the blind man would be a hero: someone whose witness grew under pressure, who lost his place in the synagogue but was found by Jesus. Fearful sympathisers would see themselves in the parents and be challenged.
chapters.today: Disability is not punishment. Faith often grows step by step through questions. The chapter also warns any community — including churches — against excluding people whose experience does not fit its expectations, and asks who is really blind.

misread.popular: The Pharisees are hard-hearted legalists who simply hated Jesus.
misread.better: The Pharisees are divided (John 9:16) and argue from Torah; the story is about how people respond to new evidence. The 'put out of the synagogue' detail likely reflects later local conflict, though the Birkat ha-Minim link is debated (Martyn, Kimelman, Marcus, Reinhartz).

chapters.title: The good shepherd and the feast of Dedication
chapters.summary: Jesus contrasts thieves and hired hands with the good shepherd who knows his sheep by name, leads them out, and lays down his life for them. 'I am the gate'; 'I am the good shepherd.' He has other sheep 'not of this fold' who will become one flock with one shepherd. Some say he is possessed; others ask whether a demon can open blind eyes. In winter, at the feast of Dedication (Hanukkah), Jesus walks in Solomon's Porch. Asked plainly if he is the Messiah, he says his works testify, his sheep hear his voice, no one will snatch them from his hand, and 'I and the Father are one'. When they move to stone him, he cites Psalm 82, 'I said, you are gods', and calls himself the one the Father consecrated and sent. He withdraws across the Jordan, where many believe.
chapters.background: The shepherd discourse follows directly from chapter 9: the authorities who threw out the healed man are contrasted with the shepherd who finds him. Hanukkah celebrated the rededication of the temple in 164 BC by Judas Maccabeus after the Seleucid king Antiochus IV had defiled it (recorded in 1 Maccabees 4, a book outside the Protestant canon). It is the only mention of Hanukkah in the Bible.
chapters.culture: Shepherds in Judea often kept several flocks together overnight in a stone fold, with one gate. In the morning each shepherd called his own sheep, which recognised his voice. Some shepherds slept across the opening as a living gate. Hired hands were paid workers without the owner's stake in the flock. Hanukkah, in winter, featured lights and the reading of the story of the Maccabees, who resisted foreign tyranny and false shepherds. Solomon's Porch, a covered colonnade on the east side of the temple, was a natural place to walk in winter.
chapters.jewishLens:
Ezekiel 34 is the key text: God condemns Israel's shepherds (its rulers) who fed themselves and not the flock, and promises, 'I myself will shepherd my sheep... I will set over them one shepherd, my servant David' (Ezek 34:11-24). Jesus claims both roles: God's own shepherding and the Davidic shepherd. Psalm 23 and Jeremiah 23:1-6 lie in the background.

At Hanukkah, the feast of the consecrated temple, Jesus says he is the one 'the Father consecrated' (hagiazō, John 10:36) — he is the dedicated temple. 'I and the Father are one' echoes the Shema, 'the Lord is one' (Deut 6:4): the sheep in his hand are in the Father's hand. His use of Psalm 82 is a rabbinic 'how much more' argument: if scripture can call those who received God's word 'gods', how much more the one God sent.
chapters.audience: A community that felt cast out would hear that the true shepherd knows them by name and that no one can snatch them away. Gentile believers would hear themselves as the 'other sheep', brought into the one flock of Israel's God, not a separate flock.
chapters.today: The picture is deeply relational: being known by name and knowing a voice. Leaders are judged by whether they lay down their lives for the flock or use it. Security rests in God's hold, not in our grip.

misread.popular: The 'other sheep' are Gentiles who form a new, separate people that replaces Israel.
misread.better: They are Gentiles (and perhaps scattered Israelites) gathered into one flock under Israel's shepherd, fulfilling Ezekiel's promise; the image is of enlargement, not replacement (Keener, Bauckham).

chapters.title: Lazarus raised and the plan to kill Jesus
chapters.summary: Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Martha and Mary, is ill. Jesus, who loves them, deliberately waits two days, and Lazarus dies. When Jesus arrives, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. Martha meets him with faith and grief; Jesus says, 'I am the resurrection and the life', and she confesses him as Messiah and Son of God. Mary weeps at his feet, and Jesus, deeply moved and angry at death, weeps too. At the tomb he prays and calls, 'Lazarus, come out!' The dead man comes out bound in grave clothes. Many believe. The chief priests and Pharisees fear the Romans will destroy 'our place and our nation'. Caiaphas says it is better that one man die for the people, which John calls an unwitting prophecy that Jesus would die to gather God's scattered children. From that day they plan to kill him.
chapters.background: In Mark the temple action triggers the plot against Jesus; in John it is the raising of Lazarus, the seventh and greatest sign. The leaders' fear (John 11:48) was realistic: Roman authorities did crush messianic movements, and by the time John wrote, Rome had in fact destroyed the temple and city in AD 70. Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36; an ornate ossuary (bone box) inscribed with the name 'Joseph son of Caiaphas', found in Jerusalem in 1990, may belong to his family.
chapters.culture: Jewish burial happened quickly, usually the same day, in a rock-cut tomb sealed with a stone. The body was washed, wrapped in cloths, with the face covered by a separate cloth. Mourning lasted seven days (shiva), and friends came to comfort the family; professional mourners might wail. Later rabbinic tradition said the soul lingered near the body for three days, so by the fourth day death was certain and decay had begun ('he stinks', John 11:39). Jesus' delay means no one could say Lazarus was merely unconscious.
chapters.jewishLens:
Martha voices the faith of many Jews, especially Pharisees: 'I know he will rise in the resurrection on the last day' (John 11:24, compare Dan 12:2). Jesus answers that the resurrection life of the last day is present in him now. The scene echoes Ezekiel's promise, 'I will open your graves... and you shall know that I am the Lord' (Ezek 37:12-13).

Caiaphas thinks politically: one man's death to save the nation from Rome. John sees in it Israel's hope of restoration: Jesus would die 'not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad' (John 11:52), the language of the ingathering of exiles (Isa 43:5-7, Ezek 37:21).
chapters.audience: Readers who had buried believers would hear Jesus' promise to Martha as their own. They would also see that Jesus' own people included those who loved him (Martha, Mary, Lazarus and the many 'Jews' who came to comfort them and believed, John 11:45).
chapters.today: Jesus does not hurry past grief; he weeps beside it, and he is angry at death. Resurrection hope is not only for the end; the life of the age to come meets people in their losses now.

misread.popular: 'The Jews' plotted Jesus' death as a people.
misread.better: Many Jews mourned with Martha and Mary and believed (John 11:45); the decision was taken by a small leadership circle fearing Rome (John 11:47-53).

chapters.title: Anointed, welcomed as king, and the hour has come
chapters.summary: Six days before Passover, at a dinner in Bethany, Mary anoints Jesus' feet with expensive perfumed oil and wipes them with her hair; Judas objects, and Jesus says she has kept it for his burial. The next day crowds with palm branches greet Jesus, shouting 'Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel', and Jesus rides a young donkey. Some Greeks ask to see Jesus, and he announces, 'The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified': like a grain of wheat, he must die to bear fruit. A voice from heaven answers his prayer. When lifted up, he will draw all people to himself. The narrator explains the unbelief of many with Isaiah, and notes that many leaders believed but did not confess it, fearing being put out of the synagogue. Jesus' final public appeal: 'I have come as light into the world.'
chapters.background: This chapter ends the 'Book of Signs'. The second aposynagōgos passage (John 12:42-43) explicitly names rulers who believed secretly because of the Pharisees, 'for they loved human glory more than the glory of God'. The arrival of Greeks marks the turning point: when Gentiles seek Jesus, his 'hour' arrives. Scholars note that John's audience included such Gentile seekers.
chapters.culture: Nard was an imported perfume from India; a pound worth 300 denarii was almost a year's wages for a labourer. Letting down her hair in public was a startling, intimate act. Palm branches were symbols of Jewish national victory; they had been waved when Simon Maccabeus liberated Jerusalem and appeared on coins of the Jewish revolts against Rome. 'Hosanna' (Hebrew 'save, please') comes from Psalm 118, sung at Passover and Sukkot. To welcome someone into the city with palms was to greet a liberating king.
chapters.jewishLens:
The crowd's cry is Ps 118:25-26, and John adds Zech 9:9: 'Do not fear, daughter of Zion; see, your king is coming, seated on a donkey's colt.' Zechariah's king comes humble and brings peace to the nations — not the warrior many hoped for. The 'lifting up' that will draw all people echoes Isaiah's servant who will be 'lifted up and greatly exalted' (Isa 52:13).

John quotes Isa 53:1 ('Lord, who has believed our report?') and Isa 6:10 (hardened eyes and hearts), and says Isaiah 'saw his glory' (John 12:41) — identifying the glory Isaiah saw on the throne with Jesus. Unbelief is explained within Israel's own prophetic story, not as a sign that Israel is rejected; Isaiah himself spoke of a people slow to see.
chapters.audience: A community that wondered why so many of their own people did not believe would find an answer in Isaiah: prophets had always met resistance. Secret believers would feel the sting of 12:43 and be urged to choose God's glory over human approval.
chapters.today: Mary's lavish love, the humble king on a donkey, and the grain that must die all point to the same truth: in John, glory is love giving itself away. Fear of losing social standing remains a powerful reason people hide what they believe.
