chapters.title: Washing feet and the new commandment
chapters.summary: Before Passover, knowing his hour has come and 'having loved his own... he loved them to the end', Jesus rises from supper, wraps a towel around himself and washes his disciples' feet. Peter refuses, then asks for a full bath; Jesus says unless he washes him, Peter has no share with him. Jesus tells them to wash one another's feet as he has done. Troubled, he announces that one of them will betray him; the Beloved Disciple, reclining next to Jesus, asks who, and Jesus gives a morsel to Judas, who goes out — 'and it was night'. Jesus says the Son of Man is now glorified, gives a new commandment, 'love one another as I have loved you', and predicts that Peter will deny him three times.
chapters.background: Here the 'Book of Glory' begins. The Beloved Disciple appears for the first time by that title (John 13:23). John dates the supper 'before the feast of Passover' (John 13:1) and Jesus' death on the day of preparation, when Passover lambs were slaughtered (John 19:14), while the Synoptics present the Last Supper as a Passover meal. Scholars have proposed different solutions: different calendars in use, John's theological choice to align Jesus' death with the lambs, or the Synoptic account being a Passover-like meal held early. John has no institution of bread and cup; the foot washing stands in its place.
chapters.culture: Guests reclined on couches around a low table, leaning on the left elbow, feet stretched away; the disciple 'at Jesus' bosom' was in a place of honour and intimacy. Feet were dusty from roads, and washing them was the job of the lowest servant; Jewish sources suggest even a Jewish slave should not be required to do it. A host might offer water, but would not wash guests' feet himself. A teacher washing his students' feet was a shocking reversal of honour.
chapters.jewishLens:
Jesus, knowing that 'the Father had given all things into his hands' (John 13:3), uses that authority to serve. The scene resembles the servant of Isaiah who humbles himself. Hospitality in Israel's stories begins with water for feet (Gen 18:4). Judas's betrayal fulfils Ps 41:9, 'He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me' — the betrayal by a table companion, a deep breach of covenant friendship.

The 'new commandment' is not new in content — 'love your neighbour as yourself' is Lev 19:18 — but new in its measure: 'as I have loved you'. It is the covenant love of the new covenant community (Jer 31:31-34), marked out as Jesus' disciples by their love.
chapters.audience: A small, pressured community needed the foot-washing more than a doctrine: humility, forgiveness and practical care for one another. Readers who had seen betrayal and failure within the group would hear that even Judas sat at the table and Peter would fall — and that Jesus' love was 'to the end'.
chapters.today: Leadership in the church is measured by the towel. The mark of Jesus' followers is not first their doctrine or culture but their love for one another, which outsiders can see.

echoes.note: The friend who ate my bread lifted his heel against me.
Love your neighbour as yourself.
Abraham offers water to wash his guests' feet.
The servant pours out his life.

misread.popular: The 'new commandment' replaces the Old Testament law of love with a new Christian ethic.
misread.better: Love of neighbour is already Torah (Lev 19:18); what is new is the pattern and power of Jesus' self-giving love in the new covenant community (Keener, Thompson).

chapters.title: The Father's house, the way, and the promised Advocate
chapters.summary: Jesus tells his troubled disciples to trust God and trust him. In his Father's house are many dwelling places; he goes to prepare a place and will come back to take them to himself. Thomas asks the way; Jesus says, 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.' Philip asks to see the Father; Jesus says whoever has seen him has seen the Father. He promises 'another Advocate' (Paraclete), the Spirit of truth, who will remain with them and teach them. He will not leave them orphans. If anyone loves him and keeps his word, the Father and he will come and make their home with that person. He gives them peace, 'not as the world gives', and says, 'Rise, let us go from here.'
chapters.background: Chapters 14-17 are the 'Farewell Discourse'. 'Rise, let us go from here' (John 14:31) followed by three more chapters of speech is one of the clues for the theory that the Gospel was edited in stages (Brown), though others see it as a deliberate literary move or a walk toward Gethsemane (Carson). The promise of the Spirit to 'remind' them of everything Jesus said (John 14:26) is also a statement about how this Gospel understood its own remembering and interpreting of Jesus.
chapters.culture: The farewell speech was a recognised Jewish genre: Jacob blesses his sons (Gen 49), Moses gives Deuteronomy before his death, David instructs Solomon (1 Kgs 2:1-9), and later Jewish 'testaments' (such as the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs) follow a pattern: announcement of departure, comfort, commands to love, warnings, promises, and appointment of successors. A paraclete in legal settings was an advocate or helper who stood beside someone. A 'house' with many rooms suggests a large extended-family household, where married sons added rooms around a shared courtyard.
chapters.jewishLens:
'My Father's house' in John 2:16 is the temple. In the temple there were many rooms (1 Kgs 6:5, Ezek 40:17) and the hope of dwelling in God's house was the hope of Psalm 23:6 and Psalm 27:4. The same word for 'dwelling place' (monē) returns in John 14:23, where the Father and Son come to dwell with the believer. So the promise is God's presence: the household of the Father, now and at Jesus' return.

'Way', 'truth' and 'life' are rich Hebrew words. The way (derek) is how one walks in Torah (Ps 119:30); truth (emet) is God's faithfulness; life is covenant blessing (Deut 30:15-20). Moses asked to see God's glory (Exod 33:18); Philip asks to see the Father, and Jesus says he has been seen in the Son. The Spirit as 'another Advocate' continues Jesus' presence as Joshua continued Moses' leadership (Deut 34:9).
chapters.audience: A community that had lost the eyewitnesses (the Beloved Disciple had died, John 21:23) and lived without Jesus' physical presence would hear: you are not orphans; the Spirit remains and teaches; the Father and Son make their home with you.
chapters.today: The famous verse 14:6 is said to anxious friends, not to opponents. It invites us to know God as Father through Jesus. The home Jesus prepares is above all a relationship — being where he is.

echoes.note: Dwelling in the house of the Lord forever.
Moses asks to see God's glory.
Moses' farewell: do not fear, God will not leave you.
'I have chosen the way of faithfulness.'
My dwelling place shall be with them.

misread.popular: Jesus promises each believer a 'mansion' in heaven after death, and 14:6 is mainly a verdict on other religions.
misread.better: 'Dwelling places' are rooms in the Father's household (compare 14:23: God dwelling with us now), with a future hope too; 14:6 is comfort to disciples about knowing the Father through Jesus, though its exclusive claim is debated in its implications (Carson, Keener, Köstenberger).

chapters.title: The true vine and the friends of Jesus
chapters.summary: Jesus says, 'I am the true vine, and my Father is the vine-grower.' Branches that bear fruit are pruned; branches cut off wither. The disciples are to remain (abide) in him as he remains in them, for apart from him they can do nothing. As the Father loved him, he has loved them; they are to remain in his love by keeping his commands, so that his joy may be in them. The greatest love is to lay down one's life for one's friends. 'I no longer call you servants... I have called you friends.' He chose them to bear lasting fruit. The world will hate them as it hated him; but the Advocate and they themselves will testify about him.
chapters.background: The Farewell Discourse continues, perhaps on the walk to the Mount of Olives. The warning that the world will hate the disciples would match the experience of John's community: rejection by neighbours, by some in the synagogue, and possibly suspicion from Roman authorities, as believers would not join in civic and imperial cults. Some scholars see chapters 15-17 as an expanded second edition of the farewell material.
chapters.culture: Vineyards were everywhere in the land of Israel. Pruning in late winter cut away dead and unfruitful wood so the vine would bear more; prunings were burned. 'Friend of the king' was a recognised court title in the ancient world for a trusted insider, and in Greco-Roman thought friendship meant frankness and shared counsel, unlike the relationship of master and slave, who is simply told what to do. Jesus elevates his followers to the status of confidants.
chapters.jewishLens:
Israel was God's vine or vineyard: 'You brought a vine out of Egypt' (Ps 80:8-16); Isaiah's song of the vineyard grieves that it produced wild grapes (Isa 5:1-7); Jeremiah calls Israel a choice vine that went wild (Jer 2:21). A golden vine decorated the entrance to Herod's temple, as Josephus describes. When Jesus calls himself 'the true vine', he is not discarding Israel but presenting himself as the faithful Israel in whom God's people are rooted. To remain in him is to belong to God's people.

Abraham and Moses were called friends of God (Isa 41:8, Exod 33:11). Jesus extends that covenant intimacy to all his disciples: they know what the master is doing.
chapters.audience: A minority under pressure needed to hear that their identity rested on staying connected to Jesus and to one another in love, that fruit would come through pruning, and that being hated did not mean being abandoned.
chapters.today: Christian life is not mainly effort but connection — remaining in a relationship of love. The status of 'friend' changes how believers relate to God: not as anxious servants but as trusted companions.

echoes.note: Israel the vine brought out of Egypt.
The song of the unfruitful vineyard.
A choice vine turned wild.
Abraham, God's friend.
God speaks to Moses face to face, as with a friend.

misread.popular: The vine replaces Israel: the church is the new vine and Israel has been cut off.
misread.better: Jesus is the faithful Israel-vine and his followers, Jewish and Gentile, are branches in him; the image is of fulfilment and belonging rather than rejection (Keener, Thompson, Bauckham).

chapters.title: Grief turned to joy and the coming Spirit
chapters.summary: Jesus warns that his disciples will be put out of synagogues, and some will even think that killing them is service to God. It is better for them that he goes away, because then the Advocate will come, who will convict the world about sin, righteousness and judgement, and will guide the disciples into all truth. In 'a little while' they will not see him, and then they will see him again. Their grief will turn to joy, as a woman's labour pain gives way to joy at a birth. They will ask the Father in Jesus' name, for the Father himself loves them. The disciples say they now understand; Jesus warns they will be scattered, yet 'take heart; I have overcome the world'.
chapters.background: John 16:2 is the third aposynagōgos passage and the most severe: exclusion and even killing. Scholars debate what this reflects. Martyn read it as the community's experience of formal expulsion; others note local tensions, the stoning of Stephen (Acts 7) and Paul's own earlier persecution of believers as a zealous Jew (Gal 1:13-14), and possible denunciation to Roman authorities. Reinhartz and others caution that we cannot simply read the community's history off the text. What is clear is that John's readers had suffered real loss and fear.
chapters.culture: Labour in childbirth was a common Jewish picture for the painful arrival of God's new age — the 'birth pangs of the Messiah'. In court, an advocate who 'convicts' brings evidence that shows who is truly in the wrong. Praying 'in the name' of someone meant praying as their representative, with their authority and character.
chapters.jewishLens:
The woman in labour echoes Isaiah's images of Zion giving birth to a new people (Isa 26:17-19, Isa 66:7-14), where birth and resurrection are linked. Those who think persecuting others is 'service to God' (latreia, worship) stand in a line of zeal for God that Paul himself once embodied; the Gospel does not mock their zeal but calls it misdirected.

The Spirit guiding into 'all truth' recalls God's promise to put his Spirit within Israel so they would walk in his ways (Ezek 36:27) and the new covenant where all will know the Lord (Jer 31:34). The disciples' 'scattering' recalls Zech 13:7, 'strike the shepherd and the sheep will be scattered'.
chapters.audience: For believers who had been expelled, threatened or bereaved, this chapter named their pain honestly and promised joy that no one could take away. It also told them their suffering was foreseen, not a sign that God had abandoned them.
chapters.today: Grief is not denied but transformed, like labour into birth. The Spirit continues Jesus' teaching presence. And the chapter warns religious people of every tradition, including Christians, that violence done 'for God' can be deeply mistaken.

echoes.note: Labour pains and the dead rising.
Zion gives birth; rejoicing replaces grief.
Strike the shepherd, the sheep scatter.
God's law written within; all will know the Lord.

misread.popular: John 16:2 shows that Jews were persecutors of Christians, so Christians are always the innocent victims.
misread.better: It reflects a specific, painful local conflict within the Jewish family; within a few centuries the power relationship reversed and Christians persecuted Jews. The text warns all who think violence is worship (Brown, Reinhartz, Levine).

chapters.title: Jesus' prayer: knowing God and being one
chapters.summary: Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven: 'Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son so that the Son may glorify you.' He defines eternal life: 'that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.' He has made the Father's name known to those the Father gave him. He prays for them: that they be kept in the Father's name, protected from the evil one, made holy in the truth, and sent into the world as he was sent. Then he prays for those who will believe through their word: that all may be one, as the Father is in him and he in the Father, so that the world may believe; and that they may be with him and see his glory, and that the Father's love may be in them.
chapters.background: Since the sixteenth-century Lutheran theologian David Chytraeus, this has been called the 'High Priestly Prayer'. It concludes the Farewell Discourse. Its concern for unity probably reflects a community that faced divisions; the letters of John speak of members who 'went out from us' (1 John 2:19). It is also the clearest single statement of John's theology of knowing God.
chapters.culture: Lifting the eyes to heaven was a common Jewish posture in prayer. In Jewish thought a 'name' stood for the person's character and presence; God put his name in the temple (Deut 12:11). To be 'kept in the name' meant to be held within God's own presence and protection.
chapters.jewishLens:
'Knowing God' in the Hebrew Bible is covenant relationship, not information: the new covenant promises that 'they shall all know me' (Jer 31:34), and Hosea mourns that there is 'no knowledge of God in the land' (Hos 4:1). Jesus defines eternal life — the life of the age to come — as that relational knowing (John 17:3), and holds firmly to Jewish monotheism: 'the only true God'.

Jesus prays like a high priest interceding for the people, consecrating himself (hagiazō) as priests and sacrifices were consecrated (Exod 28:41). His prayer that his followers be 'one' echoes the Shema's oneness (Deut 6:4) and Ezekiel's hope that God's scattered people would be gathered into one (Ezek 37:22). The glory he had 'before the world existed' links back to the Word in the beginning.
chapters.audience: A small, divided, pressured community would hear itself prayed for by name: kept, protected, consecrated and sent. Later believers ('those who will believe through their word') are also included in the prayer.
chapters.today: Christianity at its heart is knowing God as Father through Jesus. The unity Jesus prays for is a relational unity of love modelled on God himself, and it is meant to be visible to the world.

echoes.note: All shall know me, from least to greatest.
God desires the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
The Lord our God, the Lord is one.
Consecrating priests for service.
One nation, one king, no longer divided.

misread.popular: 'Eternal life' in John 17 means going to heaven forever, and unity means one institutional church or simply invisible spiritual unity.
misread.better: Eternal life is defined as knowing God now (John 17:3); unity is a visible relational oneness of love that the world can see (Thompson, Bauckham, Keener).

chapters.title: Arrest in the garden and the king before Pilate
chapters.summary: Jesus crosses the Kidron valley to a garden. Judas comes with a detachment of soldiers and temple police carrying lanterns and torches. Jesus asks whom they seek; when he says 'I am', they step back and fall to the ground. He asks them to let his disciples go. Peter cuts off the ear of Malchus, and Jesus tells him to put away his sword. Jesus is taken to Annas, former high priest, and questioned; meanwhile Peter, let into the courtyard through the Beloved Disciple's contact, denies Jesus three times by a charcoal fire. At dawn Jesus is taken to Pilate's headquarters; the accusers stay outside to avoid defilement before Passover. Pilate asks, 'Are you the king of the Jews?' Jesus says his kingdom is not from this world and that he came to testify to the truth. Pilate asks, 'What is truth?' and offers to release Jesus, but the crowd asks for Barabbas.
chapters.background: Only John mentions Roman soldiers (a speira, a cohort) at the arrest and the hearing before Annas. Annas had been high priest (AD 6-15) and five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office after him; he remained the power behind the office. The Beloved Disciple is described as 'known to the high priest' (John 18:15), which Bauckham uses to argue he was a Jerusalem disciple. Pontius Pilate governed Judea AD 26-36; an inscription bearing his name was found at Caesarea Maritima in 1961.
chapters.culture: Entering a Gentile's house could be thought to cause ritual impurity, which would prevent eating the Passover meal; the accusers stay outside, and Pilate moves in and out. The Roman governor alone had the power to execute (John 18:31), the 'right of the sword'. 'King of the Jews' was a political charge: claiming kingship without Rome's appointment was treason against Caesar. The custom of releasing a prisoner at Passover is attested only in the Gospels.
chapters.jewishLens:
The 'I am' in the garden (John 18:5-6) carries the weight of the divine name; the arresting party falls back as people fell before God's glory (Ezek 1:28). Jesus is not a helpless victim: he goes out to meet them, protects his own ('of those you gave me I lost not one', John 18:9), and accepts 'the cup the Father has given' (compare Ps 75:8, Isa 51:17).

Jesus' kingship belongs to Israel's hope: the Messiah as king (Ps 2, 2 Sam 7:12-16). 'Not from this world' means its source is God, not that it is purely spiritual or irrelevant to earth. Jesus' testimony to 'truth' (emet: God's faithful reality) stands against Pilate's cynical power.
chapters.audience: Believers facing hostile authorities, Jewish or Roman, would see their Lord standing calmly before both, in control of his own destiny. Peter's denials, beside the courageous Beloved Disciple, would comfort and warn those who had themselves failed under pressure.
chapters.today: Jesus refuses the sword. His kingdom confronts power not with violence but with testimony to truth. And even the leading apostle denies him — failure is not the end of the story (see chapter 21).

echoes.note: David crosses the Kidron in betrayal and sorrow.
'I am he' — the divine self-identification.
Rulers conspire against the Lord's anointed king.
The cup of the Lord's wrath.

misread.popular: The Jewish people as a whole demanded Jesus' death and bear collective guilt.
misread.better: John shows a small group of temple leaders with their police, plus Roman soldiers and a Roman governor; the Catholic Church's Nostra Aetate (1965) and most churches reject collective Jewish guilt (Brown, Levine).

chapters.title: Crucified king, Passover lamb, buried in a garden
chapters.summary: Pilate has Jesus flogged; soldiers mock him with a crown of thorns and a purple robe. Pilate presents him: 'Here is the man!' The chief priests cry 'Crucify!' and say 'We have no king but Caesar.' At noon on the day of preparation for Passover, Pilate hands him over. Jesus carries his own cross to Golgotha; the inscription 'Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews' is written in Hebrew, Latin and Greek. Soldiers divide his clothes and cast lots for his seamless tunic. Jesus entrusts his mother to the Beloved Disciple. He says 'I thirst', receives sour wine on hyssop, and says 'It is finished', and gives up his spirit. His legs are not broken; a soldier pierces his side, and blood and water flow out. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus bury him with about 75 pounds of myrrh and aloes in a new tomb in a garden.
chapters.background: John's timing is distinctive: Jesus is condemned around noon on the day of preparation (John 19:14), the time when Passover lambs began to be slaughtered in the temple. The narrator stresses eyewitness testimony to the blood and water: 'He who saw it has borne witness... so that you also may believe' (John 19:35). This may counter docetic ideas that Jesus only seemed to have a body. The chief priests' cry 'We have no king but Caesar' is ironic, since daily Jewish prayer confessed God alone as King.
chapters.culture:
Roman crucifixion was designed for maximum pain and public shame; it was reserved for slaves, rebels and the lowest classes. Victims were flogged first, carried the crossbeam, were often stripped, and could hang for days. The heel bone of a crucified man named Jehohanan, with an iron nail still in it, was found in a Jerusalem ossuary in 1968, confirming that nails were used and that a crucified man could receive a Jewish burial. Breaking legs (crurifragium) hastened death by suffocation; Deut 21:22-23 required bodies not to remain overnight, especially before a Sabbath and feast day.

Jewish burial for an honoured person involved spices and linen. 'A hundred litrai' (about 75 pounds) of spices is a royal quantity; Josephus describes lavish spices at Herod's funeral. A garden tomb belonged to the wealthy.
chapters.jewishLens:
Jesus dies as the Passover lamb: hyssop was used to put the lamb's blood on the doorposts (Exod 12:22), and none of the lamb's bones were to be broken (Exod 12:46, Num 9:12). John the Baptist's 'Lamb of God' (John 1:29) is fulfilled. The piercing fulfils Zech 12:10, 'they will look on the one they have pierced', a passage about mourning in Jerusalem that leads to cleansing (Zech 13:1). The divided garments echo Ps 22:18, the psalm of the righteous sufferer.

The seamless tunic may recall the high priest's woven robe (Exod 28:32). Blood and water may point to the temple's sacrifice and the river of living water (Ezek 47:1, John 7:38). 'It is finished' (tetelestai) means accomplished: the work the Father gave is complete (John 17:4). And at the cross a new family is created: the mother of Jesus and the Beloved Disciple are given to each other as mother and son.
chapters.audience: Readers would see that the shameful cross was in fact the 'lifting up' of a king and the Passover of the world. Those who had been afraid would take heart from Joseph and Nicodemus, secret disciples who finally stepped forward at the most dangerous moment.
chapters.today: The glory of God is seen in a crucified man who cares for his mother in his agony. In John the cross is not defeat but completion. It also forms a new family that crosses blood ties.

echoes.note: No bone of the Passover lamb broken.
Hyssop used for the lamb's blood.
They divide my garments and cast lots.
They will look on the one whom they pierced.
For my thirst they gave me vinegar.

misread.popular: 'We have no king but Caesar' shows the Jewish nation rejecting God and being rejected.
misread.better: The words are spoken by the chief priests (John 19:15), a small leadership group; John presents them as tragic irony, not a verdict on the Jewish people (Brown, Keener, Levine).

chapters.title: The garden, the breath of life, and Thomas's confession
chapters.summary: Early on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene finds the stone removed and runs to Peter and the Beloved Disciple. They run to the tomb; the Beloved Disciple arrives first; Peter goes in and sees the linen cloths lying and the face-cloth rolled up separately. The Beloved Disciple 'saw and believed'. Mary stays weeping, sees two angels, then Jesus, whom she takes for the gardener — until he says 'Mary', and she answers 'Rabbouni!' He sends her to tell his 'brothers': 'I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.' That evening Jesus appears to the disciples behind locked doors, says 'Peace be with you', shows his wounds, sends them as the Father sent him, breathes on them and says, 'Receive the Holy Spirit.' Thomas, absent, refuses to believe without touching the wounds. A week later Jesus invites him, and Thomas confesses, 'My Lord and my God!' Jesus blesses those who have not seen and yet believe. John states his purpose: these things are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and have life in his name.
chapters.background: Mary Magdalene is the first witness to the risen Jesus, and the Latin tradition later called her the 'apostle to the apostles' (Hippolytus and later writers). In the ancient world women's testimony was often given less weight in court, which many historians count as a reason the story was not invented. John 20:30-31 looks like the original ending of the Gospel; chapter 21 follows as an epilogue. There is a textual variant in 20:31: 'that you may come to believe' (aorist) or 'that you may continue to believe' (present); the manuscripts are divided, and scholars debate whether the book is mainly evangelistic or for strengthening believers.
chapters.culture: The 'first day of the week' is Sunday, the day after the Sabbath. Tombs were often in gardens or orchards, so a gardener would be a natural person to meet. 'Rabbouni' is an Aramaic form of 'my teacher', and the narrator translates it for Greek-speaking readers. 'Peace be with you' (shalom aleichem) was the ordinary Jewish greeting, but now filled with new meaning after the cross.
chapters.jewishLens:
The garden setting recalls Eden; the risen Jesus is mistaken for the gardener, the role of the first Adam (Gen 2:15). When he breathes on the disciples, John uses the same rare verb (emphysaō) as the Greek translation of Gen 2:7, where God breathed life into Adam, and Ezek 37:9, where the Spirit breathes on the dry bones. This is new creation: a new humanity and a restored Israel.

'My Father and your Father, my God and your God' (John 20:17) echoes Ruth's covenant pledge, 'your people shall be my people, and your God my God' (Ruth 1:16): the disciples are now Jesus' 'brothers' in God's family. Thomas's 'My Lord and my God' answers the prologue's 'the Word was God' and applies to Jesus the language Israel used for its God (Ps 35:23).
chapters.audience: Readers who had never seen Jesus would hear themselves blessed in John 20:29. Thomas gives permission to doubt honestly. The purpose statement tells them directly why the book exists: for their ongoing trust and their life.
chapters.today: Jesus meets people personally — calling Mary by name, inviting Thomas to touch. Resurrection is the start of a new creation, and the Spirit is given for mission: 'as the Father has sent me, so I send you.'

echoes.note: God breathes the breath of life into Adam.
Breath enters the slain and they live.
Seeking the one my soul loves and finding him.
'Your God my God' — covenant belonging.
'My God and my Lord' addressed to Israel's God.

chapters.title: Breakfast by the sea and Peter restored
chapters.summary: By the Sea of Tiberias (Galilee), seven disciples fish all night and catch nothing. At dawn a stranger on the shore tells them to cast the net on the right side; they haul in 153 large fish and the net does not tear. The Beloved Disciple says, 'It is the Lord!' Peter jumps into the sea. Jesus has a charcoal fire with fish and bread and invites them to breakfast. Afterward he asks Peter three times, 'Do you love me?' and three times commissions him: 'Feed my lambs; tend my sheep; feed my sheep.' He foretells that Peter will die by being bound and led where he does not want to go. Peter asks about the Beloved Disciple; Jesus says, 'If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you? Follow me.' The narrator corrects a rumour that this disciple would not die, and the community affirms: 'We know that his testimony is true.'
chapters.background: Most scholars see chapter 21 as an epilogue added after 20:31, possibly by the same author or by the community after the Beloved Disciple's death; Bauckham argues it was planned by the author as a balancing epilogue to the prologue. The correction of the rumour (John 21:23) suggests the Beloved Disciple had died or was very old, which troubled those who expected him to live until Jesus returned. Peter's death, foretold here, is traditionally placed in Rome under Nero, around AD 64-67 (1 Clement 5, a source outside the canon).
chapters.culture: Fishing on the Sea of Galilee was usually done at night with drag nets or casting nets. Peter, stripped for work, puts on his outer garment before jumping in — perhaps out of respect, to greet his master properly. A charcoal fire (anthrakia) is mentioned only twice in the New Testament: the fire where Peter denied Jesus (John 18:18) and this one. A shared meal in the ancient world was an act of reconciliation and restored relationship.
chapters.jewishLens:
Peter's threefold denial is answered by a threefold restoration, and his commission is in shepherding language: God's people as a flock entrusted to faithful leaders, in contrast to the bad shepherds of Ezekiel 34 and in line with the shepherd of John 10. Jesus feeding the disciples with bread and fish recalls the feeding in John 6 and God providing for his people in the wilderness.

The 153 fish have produced many symbolic interpretations (Jerome said Greek zoologists counted 153 species of fish, suggesting all nations; others note 153 is the 'triangular number' of 17, or link it to Ezek 47:10, where fishermen spread nets from En-gedi to En-eglaim beside the life-giving river). Many scholars think it may simply be an eyewitness memory, while the unbroken net suggests a mission that gathers without breaking.
chapters.audience: For a community grieving its founding witness and perhaps uncertain about its relation to the wider church led by Peter's memory, the chapter honours both: Peter as shepherd, the Beloved Disciple as witness. Each disciple has his own calling: 'What is that to you? Follow me.'
chapters.today: Failure is not final. Jesus restores Peter not with a lecture but with breakfast and the question 'Do you love me?' Leadership flows from love and means feeding others. And comparing callings is pointless; each disciple must simply follow.

echoes.note: Fishermen with many fish beside the river of life.
Shepherds who fail to feed the flock.
God sends many fishermen to gather his people.
A table prepared, a restored guest.

misread.popular: The two Greek words for love (agapaō and phileō) prove that Peter could only offer an inferior 'friendship' love.
misread.better: John uses the two verbs interchangeably elsewhere (e.g. both for the Father's love of the Son, John 3:35 and John 5:20); most scholars (Carson, Keener, Brown) see stylistic variation. The point is the threefold restoration.

misreadings.topic: 'The Jews' as the whole Jewish people
misreadings.popular: Many readers, hearing phrases like 'the Jews sought to kill him' (John 5:18), take John to be describing the Jewish people as a whole as Jesus' enemies. In older Christian preaching this fed the charge that 'the Jews killed Christ'.
misreadings.inContext: Ioudaioi in John has several senses: Judeans, the Jewish people generally, and most often the temple-based authorities in Jerusalem. The same Gospel says 'salvation is from the Jews' (John 4:22), says many Jews believed (John 11:45, John 12:11), and has Jewish characters on both sides. Jesus, his family and disciples are all Jews; the very people afraid 'of the Jews' are Jews themselves (John 7:13). Scholars such as Raymond Brown, Craig Keener and Amy-Jill Levine stress this. Adele Reinhartz, a Jewish New Testament scholar, goes further: she argues that even read carefully John's rhetoric distances believers from 'the Jews' and has an anti-Jewish effect, and that honesty requires admitting this rather than explaining it away.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical commentators such as D. A. Carson and Andreas Köstenberger fully reject antisemitic use of John and agree 'the Jews' usually means the leaders who opposed Jesus. Some add that 'the Jews' can also stand for the unbelieving 'world' as a theological category, and that John's strong words are a prophetic, intra-Jewish critique like those in Isaiah or Jeremiah, not ethnic hatred. Some translations now render it 'the Judeans' or 'the Jewish leaders' where context supports it, though others warn that this can hide a real difficulty.
misreadings.whyItMatters: John was quoted in sermons, passion plays and propaganda that led to violence against Jewish people. Reading Ioudaioi carefully is a matter of truth and of love of neighbour.

misreadings.popular: John 3:16 is often presented on its own as the whole gospel in one verse: God loves you, believe in Jesus, and you will go to heaven when you die.
misreadings.inContext: John 3:16 is the climax of a sentence that begins in John 3:14: 'as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up'. In Num 21:4-9 dying Israelites looked at the bronze serpent and lived. 'So' (houtōs) in 3:16 mainly means 'in this way': God loved the world in this manner, by giving his Son to be lifted up on the cross. 'Eternal life' is the life of the age to come, starting now. 'The world' in John is humanity alienated from God, which makes the love more surprising. Scholars such as Craig Keener and Marianne Meye Thompson stress the Numbers background.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars (Carson, Köstenberger) agree on the Numbers background and the meaning 'in this way', and would say the popular use is not wrong but thin: God's love, the gift of the Son, and life through trust are all in the verse. They also point out that John does speak of future resurrection (John 5:28-29, John 6:40), so the 'after death' hope is real, not a mistake.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Reconnecting 3:16 to the cross and to Israel's wilderness story keeps the love of God from becoming sentimental: it is costly, cross-shaped love that heals the deadly bite of sin.

misreadings.topic: 'Born again' as a one-time decision formula
misreadings.popular: 'You must be born again' (John 3:3) is often understood as a moment of personal decision, praying a prayer to receive Christ, after which one is a 'born-again Christian'.
misreadings.inContext: Anōthen means both 'again' and 'from above'; Nicodemus hears 'again', but Jesus means 'from above' — a birth God causes by the Spirit (John 1:13). The background is Ezekiel's promise of water and Spirit to renew Israel (Ezek 36:25-27) and the valley of dry bones (Ezek 37). It is about God creating a renewed people, not a human technique. And Nicodemus himself does not 'decide' in one scene; he reappears gradually (John 7:50-51, John 19:39). Keener, Thompson and Brown emphasise the Ezekiel background.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars agree new birth is God's work, not a formula, and Reformed theologians in particular insist regeneration precedes faith. Many would still say the new birth is a real beginning that becomes visible in a moment of turning, and that conversion experiences are a legitimate way people come into the new life. The problem is not the idea of a beginning but treating a prayer as the cause rather than the Spirit.
misreadings.whyItMatters: New birth as God's re-creation of a people keeps the focus on the Spirit's ongoing work and on a life of trust, rather than on a past event as a ticket.

misreadings.popular: From the King James 'In my Father's house are many mansions', many picture individual luxury homes in heaven that Jesus is building for believers to enjoy after death.
misreadings.inContext: 'Mansions' is from Latin mansiones, 'dwelling places' or 'rooms'. 'My Father's house' in John 2:16 is the temple, and the image may be of rooms in the temple or in a large family house. The same word monē returns in John 14:23 where the Father and Son come and make their 'dwelling' with the believer now. The promise is about belonging in God's household, at home with the Father, rather than real estate. Some scholars (e.g. Mary Coloe) connect it to the temple; others note Jewish wedding customs of a groom preparing rooms, though that link is uncertain.
misreadings.defence: Carson and others agree 'mansions' is a mistranslation in modern English, but maintain that 14:2-3 does refer to Jesus' future return and believers being with him, so a future hope is truly in view. The best reading holds both: dwelling with God now by the Spirit (14:23) and fully at his coming.
misreadings.whyItMatters: The promise is not a better house but a closer relationship: the Father's home is wherever he is with his children.

misreadings.popular: 'You are of your father the devil' has been quoted for centuries as if Jesus were saying Jews as a people are children of the devil.
misreadings.inContext: In context Jesus is speaking to 'the Jews who had believed in him' (John 8:31) and who now want to kill him (John 8:40). The point is moral parentage: whoever seeks murder and lies shows whose family they belong to, the same logic used by Jewish prophets and by the Dead Sea Scrolls (which speak of 'sons of light' and 'sons of darkness' inside Israel). 1 John 3:8-10 applies the same test to anyone who claims to be a Christian. Brown, Keener and Levine all stress that this is polemic within the Jewish family. Reinhartz warns that, however it began, its effect on later readers was devastating.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars agree it cannot be applied to Jews as a people and condemn its antisemitic use. They read it as a spiritual diagnosis that applies to all who reject truth, Gentile or Jew, and note that the same chapter has Jesus say 'Abraham rejoiced to see my day' — he does not reject Abraham's family but claims to be its fulfilment.
misreadings.whyItMatters: This verse was used in medieval and Nazi propaganda. Reading it in its setting is a basic act of justice.

misreadings.topic: John 14:6 and the question of other religions
misreadings.popular: 'No one comes to the Father except through me' is often used as a proof text that all people of other faiths are excluded from salvation, sometimes in a combative way.
misreadings.inContext: Jesus says this to his own frightened disciples on the night before his death, in answer to Thomas's 'we do not know the way'. In Jewish idiom 'the way' (derek) is how one walks with God (Ps 119:30), and 'truth' (emet) is covenant faithfulness. Jesus is saying he is the path to the Father's home of 14:2: in knowing him they know the Father (John 14:7-9). It is a statement of comfort and identity, not originally an argument with other religions. Scholars differ on what follows for people who never hear of Jesus.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars (Carson, Köstenberger) maintain the verse really is exclusive: there is no access to the Father apart from Jesus, and that is consistent with Acts 4:12. Inclusivist evangelicals (e.g. Clark Pinnock) agree Jesus is the only way but argue he may save some who do not know his name. Both sides agree the verse should be spoken with the tenderness of its setting, not as a weapon.
misreadings.whyItMatters: The verse's original tone matters: it is an invitation to know God as Father through Jesus, said by a man about to die for his friends.

misreadings.popular: Readers divide: some read 'born of water and the Spirit' as baptism, others as physical birth (amniotic water) followed by spiritual birth.
misreadings.inContext: Jesus rebukes Nicodemus as 'the teacher of Israel' for not understanding (John 3:10), which suggests the answer lies in Israel's scriptures: Ezek 36:25-27 joins clean water and a new spirit as God's cleansing and renewal of his people. 'Water and Spirit' then likely describes one birth: cleansing and renewal by God. Many scholars (Carson, Keener) favour this; Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant readers also see a reference to baptism, as did the early church. The physical-birth reading has fewer defenders among scholars.
misreadings.defence: Sacramental traditions argue that John's readers knew Christian baptism and would hear it here, especially since John 3:22 mentions baptising. Evangelicals who read Ezekiel can agree that baptism later expresses this cleansing without being its cause. This is a genuine scholarly disagreement, not just a popular error.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Knowing the Ezekiel background shows that new birth is God's promised renewal of Israel now opened to all.

misreadings.topic: 'Eternal life' as only life after death
misreadings.popular: 'Eternal life' is often heard as endless existence in heaven that begins at death.
misreadings.inContext: In Jewish thought the two ages were 'this age' and 'the age to come' (Dan 12:2). Zōē aiōnios is the life of that coming age. John's distinctive point is that it starts now: whoever trusts 'has' eternal life and 'has passed from death to life' (John 5:24). Jesus defines it as knowing God (John 17:3) — a relationship. Thompson, Bauckham and Keener emphasise this.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars agree strongly with this 'already' emphasis and note that John also keeps a 'not yet' — resurrection on the last day (John 6:39-40). So the popular view is incomplete rather than wrong.
misreadings.whyItMatters: If eternal life starts now, Christian life is about present friendship with God and love for others, not only waiting to leave the world.

misreadings.topic: John as a 'Greek' or anti-Jewish Gospel
misreadings.popular: Older scholarship and some popular teaching said John's Logos came from Greek philosophy and that John is the least Jewish Gospel, written for Gentiles to replace Judaism.
misreadings.inContext: Since the Dead Sea Scrolls (light/darkness, truth, spirit of truth) and wider study of Second Temple Judaism, most scholars see John as deeply Jewish. Its Logos draws on Gen 1, Wisdom (Prov 8, and the Wisdom of Solomon and Sirach in the Apocrypha), and Jewish thinkers like Philo. Daniel Boyarin, a Jewish Talmud scholar, has argued that the prologue is a Jewish midrash on Genesis using a Logos/Memra theology that some Jews already held. Raymond Brown and Craig Keener also stress the Jewish background.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars welcome the recovery of John's Jewishness, and many argue it supports the reliability of its traditions (Köstenberger, Carson, Bauckham). Some note that John still deliberately addresses a wider Greek-speaking audience, for whom 'Logos' also had resonance, so it is 'both/and'.
misreadings.whyItMatters: If John is Jewish to its core, Christians cannot read it as a charter against Judaism; it is a Jewish argument about Israel's God and Israel's Messiah.

perspectives.name: Traditional apostolic authorship
perspectives.who: Irenaeus (c. 180) and later church tradition; modern defenders include D. A. Carson, Andreas Köstenberger, Craig Blomberg, Leon Morris.
perspectives.summary: The Beloved Disciple is John son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve, who wrote (or dictated) the Gospel in Ephesus in old age, perhaps in the 90s. The Gospel's detailed knowledge of Jerusalem and Palestinian geography (the pool of Bethesda, Solomon's Porch, Jacob's well) fits an eyewitness.
perspectives.strengths: Strong second-century tradition (Irenaeus, who knew Polycarp); the Beloved Disciple is close to Peter, as John is in Mark and Acts; the son of Zebedee is never named in the Gospel, which is odd unless he is the author; accurate topographical details confirmed by archaeology (e.g. the pool of Bethesda with five porticoes).
perspectives.critiques: The Gospel never names its author; Acts 4:13 calls John 'unlettered'; the Gospel lacks scenes where the son of Zebedee is present in the Synoptics (Transfiguration, Jairus' daughter); Papias seems to distinguish an apostle John from an 'elder John', and Irenaeus may have merged them.

perspectives.name: Johannine community (multi-stage composition)
perspectives.who: J. Louis Martyn, Raymond Brown (The Community of the Beloved Disciple), many critical scholars in the late twentieth century.
perspectives.summary: The Gospel grew in stages within a community gathered around the Beloved Disciple. It can be read on two levels: the story of Jesus and the later story of the community, especially its expulsion from the synagogue (the aposynagōgos passages, John 9:22, John 12:42, John 16:2), which Martyn linked to the Birkat ha-Minim, a synagogue benediction against heretics.
perspectives.strengths: Explains rough transitions (e.g. 'Rise, let us go from here' at John 14:31 followed by three more chapters), the apparent ending at 20:31 plus chapter 21, and the bitterness toward synagogue authorities as reflecting real trauma.
perspectives.critiques: The Birkat ha-Minim cannot be shown to have targeted Christians in the first century (Reuven Kimelman, 1981); reading a community history out of a Gospel is speculative; Bauckham argues the Gospels were written for wide circulation, not single communities; Reinhartz critiques the 'expulsion' theory itself.

perspectives.name: Eyewitness testimony (Bauckham)
perspectives.who: Richard Bauckham (Jesus and the Eyewitnesses, The Testimony of the Beloved Disciple); in part Martin Hengel.
perspectives.summary: The Beloved Disciple was a real eyewitness, but not one of the Twelve: John the Elder, a Jerusalem disciple mentioned by Papias, who later lived in Ephesus. He wrote the Gospel himself as a deliberate testimony, and 'we know that his testimony is true' (John 21:24) is a claim of historiographic eyewitness.
perspectives.strengths: Fits Papias' two Johns; explains the Jerusalem focus and the disciple 'known to the high priest' (John 18:15); takes the Gospel's own self-presentation seriously; explains why the Beloved Disciple is absent from Galilean Synoptic scenes.
perspectives.critiques: Traditionalists say it rejects Irenaeus too quickly; critical scholars say it trusts Papias and the Gospel's claims too much; the identification remains a hypothesis.

perspectives.name: Jewish-Christian intramural conflict
perspectives.who: Wayne Meeks, Raymond Brown, Craig Keener, Amy-Jill Levine and many others in different ways; Daniel Boyarin argues 'Judaism' and 'Christianity' were not yet fully separate.
perspectives.summary: John is the record of a painful argument within the Jewish family about whether Jesus is Israel's Messiah and how he relates to the one God. Its polemic is like the sharp language between Jewish groups in the Dead Sea Scrolls. The 'parting of the ways' had not fully happened.
perspectives.strengths: Takes seriously that everyone in the story is Jewish; explains both John's deep Jewishness and its harshness; offers a way to read John without antisemitism.
perspectives.critiques: Adele Reinhartz argues that calling it 'intramural' can soften the Gospel's real anti-Jewish effect, since John itself creates distance from 'the Jews'; others question how much of the community history can be known.

perspectives.name: Historically reliable but theologically shaped
perspectives.who: Paul N. Anderson (John, Jesus and History project), Craig Keener, Craig Blomberg; earlier C. H. Dodd.
perspectives.summary: John is an independent tradition about Jesus, not just a theological meditation built on the Synoptics. Some of its details (a ministry of several years, multiple visits to Jerusalem, the dating of the crucifixion on the eve of Passover) may be more historically accurate than the Synoptics, while its discourses are shaped in John's own voice.
perspectives.strengths: Explains confirmed details (Bethesda, the pool of Siloam excavated in 2004); fits the different style of Jesus' speech as interpreted testimony.
perspectives.critiques: Sceptical scholars think the discourses are mostly the evangelist's creation; conservatives worry 'shaped' concedes too much.

keyTerms.usual: A spoken word; or a Greek philosophical idea of cosmic reason.
keyTerms.inContext: God's creative and revealing speech (Gen 1, Ps 33:6), close to Wisdom (Prov 8) and the Aramaic Memra used in the Targums for God acting. John says this Word is personal, was with God and was God, and became flesh.
'Pitched his tent', recalling the tabernacle (skēnē) and the Shekinah glory. Jesus is God's dwelling with Israel.
Likely echoes hesed ve'emet, 'steadfast love and faithfulness', God's covenant character revealed to Moses (Exod 34:6). It is relational loyalty, not just ideas.

keyTerms.usual: A simple 'It's me' or an introduction to a metaphor.
keyTerms.inContext: Seven 'I am' sayings with images (bread, light, door, shepherd, resurrection, way, vine) and several absolute 'I am' sayings that echo God's self-naming in Exod 3:14 and Isaiah's 'I am he'.
A deed that points beyond itself to Jesus' identity, like Moses' signs in Egypt (Exod 4:8-9). John chooses seven to tell the story.

keyTerms.usual: Agreeing that something is true; a one-time decision.
keyTerms.inContext: Ongoing trust and loyalty toward a person, often joined to 'remain' and 'follow'. John uses the verb roughly 98 times and never the noun.

keyTerms.usual: Living forever in heaven after death.
keyTerms.inContext: The life of the age to come (Dan 12:2), begun now through knowing God and Jesus (John 17:3), completed at the resurrection.

keyTerms.usual: The Jewish people as a whole.
keyTerms.inContext: Context-dependent: Judeans, the Jewish people at feasts, or, frequently, the Jerusalem authorities hostile to Jesus. Used about 70 times in John.
Found only in John (three times). Probably reflects real exclusion of Jesus-followers from local synagogue communities; whether this was formal or empire-wide is debated.
One called alongside: an advocate or helper, the Spirit of truth who continues Jesus' presence and witness, as Joshua continued Moses or Elisha Elijah.

keyTerms.usual: Staying in church or keeping saved.
keyTerms.inContext: Staying close in a relationship; making one's home with someone. The Father and Son make their dwelling (monē) with disciples.
God's visible presence (kavod) in tabernacle and temple, now seen above all in Jesus being 'lifted up' on the cross.
Jesus' appointed hour of death and glorification; 'not yet come' in early chapters, 'has come' from John 12:23.
Deliberately double: 'again' and 'from above'. Jesus means a birth caused by God's Spirit.
